Learning Objectives
Review bearing surface options for primary and revision total hip arthroplasty.
Understand bearing surface influence on total hip arthroplasty stability.
Appreciate the complications and wear rates of different bearing surface options for total hip
arthroplasty.

The bearing surface articulation between the femoral and acetabular components is an
important consideration in total hip arthroplasty (THA) because it has considerable
implications with regard to component wear, implant longevity, joint stability, and
treatment options at the time of revision surgery. Component wear at the bearing
surface is a common cause of late THA failure, and the secondary effects of particle
generation are associated with osteolysis, loosening, metallosis, and local tissue
reactions. In addition, dislocation remains a substantial challenge after THA and is a
frequent indication for revision surgery. Multiple factors can influence the rates of
dislocation, including component positioning, the surgical approach, prior hip surgery,
spinal stiffness, and patient-related issues. Several bearing surface options have been
developed to improve implant longevity, reduce wear, decrease the risk of dislocation
and to provide treatment options at the time of revision surgery for patients with well-
positioned components. Orthopaedic surgeons should be aware of several common
bearing surface options, their relative indications, and clinical outcomes.
Tribology
Background
Tribology is the science of wear and friction between interacting surfaces, and is particularly
important to consider in component selection for THA.
In the hip, the spherical femoral head articulates against a concave, hemispherical acetabular
component. The head and the acetabular surface may be made of distinct or similar materials
and may be soft (polyethylene) or hard (metal or ceramic).

Tribology
The various combination of surface hardness and material properties are associated
with distinct advantages and disadvantages and may determine implant longevity.
Indications

To balance longevity and short-term complications, most THA bearing surfaces currently
implanted include a hard head that articulates against a soft acetabulum.
Popular THA articulation options
o
A metal head against a highly cross-linked polyethylene acetabulum
o
A ceramic head against a highly cross-linked polyethylene acetabulum
o
Dual mobility; adds a second articulation between the polyethylene and a metal shell
Rarely used or historic options
o
A ceramic head on a ceramic acetabulum
o
Conventional polyethylene
o
A metal head on a smooth metal acetabulum
Clinical Outcomes

Clinical Outcomes
Metal heads articulating against traditional polyethylene acetabular cups were popular
after their introduction in the 1960s and resulted in good outcomes;1 however, these
articulations also led to a high degree of polyethylene wear, with microscopic plastic
debris released as a result of the friction between the head and the acetabulum. These
microscopic plastic particles may lead to osteolysis and, ultimately, component failure.
This type of osteolysis from volumetric wear debris is thought to be the main reason for
late revision THA and may be the limiting factor affecting the lifespan of implants that
involve the use of such an articulation. This led to the introduction of cross-linked
polyethylene, which has replaced conventional polyethylene in THA.2 Cross-linked
polyethylene liners are associated with much lower wear rates compared with non–
cross-linked polyethylene.3 Switching the metal femoral head to a smoother ceramic
head further decreased volumetric wear.4
Some laboratory results raised concerns with regard to the wear resistance of cross-
linked polyethylene in less-than-ideal situations (i.e., against roughened surfaces or
third-body wear.5 For example, the scratch height and width of cross-linked polyethylene
liners against metal debris trend higher compared with that of conventional
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:26 AM
AAOS | Bearing Surface Options: Wear, Stability, and Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002061
3/31

polyethylene.6 In addition, concern existed that cross-linked polyethylene debris was
more immunogenic, resulting in an increase in its inflammatory potential per volume of
wear compared with that of traditional high-molecular-weight polyethylene.7 However,
the improved wear properties of cross-linked polyethylene far outpaced these potential
pitfalls, and the advantages of cross-linked polyethylene acetabular liners articulating
with a metal or ceramic head bearing surface is reflected in the nearly universal
adoption of such implants in the United States, comprising 98% of the THA implants
used in 2012.2
Metal-on-metal bearing surfaces showed early promise and adoption but largely have
been abandoned.2 Metal-on-metal wear rates are comparable with those of
polyethylene.8 All-metal components also allowed for thinner implants and bone-
preserving resurfacing constructs; however, metal-on-metal bearings result in much
smaller ionic wear particles and, therefore, a much higher volume of particles, at a rate
13 to 500 times greater than that of metal-on-polyethylene bearings.9 This local build-up
of metal debris in the tissues (metallosis) can produce a T-cell response and aseptic
lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesions.10 This inflammatory reaction may
cause pseudotumor formation, resulting in premature failure of THA.11
Ceramic-on-ceramic articulations also are available. The smoothness between the
acetabulum and the head generates the least amount of friction of any bearing couple.12
The hardness of the ceramic results in the least amount of wear compared with all
available materials,13 and ceramic appears to result in little surface damage from third-
body particles.14 Ceramic itself is inert and biocompatible.15 Concerns with regard to
using a ceramic-on-ceramic bearing include catastrophic failure during fracture and
squeaking,16 as well as much higher costs.
Conclusion

The most popular bearing surfaces currently implanted are not too dissimilar from the
original Charnley low-friction THA implant; however, advances in the manufacturing of
polyethylene have resulted in modern, highly cross-linked polyethylene, which is
associated with superior wear proprieties. This new polyethylene is coupled with a hard
femoral head that is polished metal or ceramic.
Femoral Head Size
Background
Multiple techniques are available for the management of instability intraoperatively and
postoperatively. Intraoperative techniques focus on achieving an optimal component position,
restoring appropriate leg length and offset, selecting a femoral head size and liner style, and
avoiding component and bony impingement.
Increased femoral head size is a method that can be used to improve stability in THA.
Larger head size increases the head-neck ratio.
Increased angle to impingement
Increased angle of dislocation
Increased jump distance
Disadvantages of larger head size
Volumetric wear
Thinner polyethylene liners
Taper corrosion

Background
Jump distance is defined as the distance that the head must travel before dislocation
from the acetabular component. Larger femoral heads are seated deeper within the
acetabulum, thereby increasing the jump distance17 (Figure 1). For every 1 mm increase
in head diameter, the jump distance increases by 0.4 mm at 45° of hip abduction.18

Figure 1 Schematic drawings show the beneficial effect of a larger femoral head on the
jump distance. Hypothetically, for a horizontal cup with a concentric center of rotation,
the jump distance is equal to the radius of the femoral head. A, For a 22-mm diameter
femoral head, the translation necessary for dislocation is 11 mm. B, For a 40-mm
femoral head, the translation necessary for dislocation is 20 mm. (Courtesy of Murillo
Adrados, MD, Roanoke, VA.)
The angle to impingement is defined as the hip angle that can be reached before
impingement of the neck onto the acetabular component occurs or before bony
impingement occurs between the femur and pelvis.19 Computer models have shown
that a larger head size (up to 36 mm) allows for increased range of motion before
component impingement. With ideally placed components, extra-articular bony
impingement becomes the limiting factor with head sizes larger than 32 mm20 (Figure
2).
Figure 2 Schematic drawings show that a larger femoral head size increases not only the
jump distance but also the head-neck ratio (A), which allows for a greater arc of motion
before component impingement (B). (Courtesy of Murillo Adrados, MD, Roanoke, VA.)
The angle of dislocation is defined as the hip angle that can be reached before
dislocation of the component.19 Dislocation may result from component impingement
and/or bony impingement. The angle of dislocation continues to increase with a head
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:26 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002061
6/31

size larger than 32 mm, even if bone-on-bone impingement restricts range of motion,
because of increased jump distance17 (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Schematic drawings show the difference between the angle to impingement (A)
and the angle to dislocation (B). The angle to impingement is the arc of motion that will
produce contact between the trunnion and the acetabular component. The angle to
dislocation reflects the angle to impingement and the jump distance. (Courtesy of
Murillo Adrados, MD, Roanoke, VA.)
The literature is mixed on the volumetric wear of highly cross-linked polyethylene with
increasing head sizes. Some studies have shown similar linear wear but greater
volumetric wear with head sizes of 36 mm or larger compared with head sizes of 32
mm.21,22Other studies have shown no substantial difference in linear or volumetric wear
rates.23-25
Larger head sizes inherently require the polyethylene liner to be thinner to fit into the
acetabular shell (Figure 4, A). The wear characteristics of modern, highly cross-linked
polyethylene liners are excellent;25,26 however, failure of the component occurs with
less wear in patients with a thinner polyethylene liner. In addition, highly cross-linked
polyethylene has reduced fracture toughness and a lower tolerance of component
malpositioning, which may be of greater concern with thinner liners. A minimum liner
thickness of 5 to 6 mm generally is recommended, regardless of bearing type.27
Surgeons must be mindful of polyethylene thickness, particularly in younger patients.

Figure 4 Schematic drawings show the disadvantages of a larger femoral head. A, For
the same size cup, a larger femoral head requires a thinner polyethylene liner, which
predisposes the implant a shorter life expectancy with regard to wear. This also
increases the risk of catastrophic failure (the plastic breaking). B, Laboratory tests show
that larger femoral heads result in more volumetric wear because an increased arc of
motion occurs at the surface of the femoral head with the same range of motion of the
leg; the surface travels farther with the same arc of motion, which results in more
attrition between the femoral head and acetabulum and, therefore, accelerated wear. C,
With the same linear wear, a larger femoral head results in a higher volume of
polyethylene particles; therefore, a greater cylinder of polyethylene is lost. D, Torque at
the trunnion-head interface increases as femoral head size increases because of the
higher moment arm between the trunnion and the tangential forces at the femoral head
surface, which correlates with higher corrosion at the trunnion. (Courtesy of Murillo
Adrados, MD, Roanoke, VA.)
Some controversy exists in the literature with regard to the effect of head size on taper
corrosion and fretting28 (Figure 4, D). Some retrieval studies have shown greater
corrosion and fretting with 36-mm heads than with 28-mm heads, which is thought to
result from greater torque along the taper interface.29 Other studies have not shown the

8/31

same association between head size and taper corrosion.30,31 Multiple studies have
shown that ceramic heads result in substantially lower fretting and corrosion than
cobalt-chromium heads.32,33 Based on this data, using ceramic with larger head sizes
should be considered.
Indications
A head size that provides the greatest stability should be selected, considering the potential
consequences of a thinner polyethylene liners, volumetric wear, and taper corrosion
associated with larger heads.
Based on registry data, the most common femoral head sizes currently used are 32 mm and
36 mm.34
Head sizes of 40 mm or larger rarely are indicated because these head sizes have not been
shown to improve stability compared with 32-mm or 36-mm heads and these larger head
sizes may be associated with higher rates of volumetric wear and taper corrosion.
Different component systems allow for various possible head sizes, depending on the specific
acetabular shell and polyethylene liner implanted.
The minimum recommended liner thickness is 5 to 6 mm.27
The most appropriate head size for the system being used should be selected to optimize
stability based on final cup size and anticipated polyethylene liner thickness, as well as
patient age, health status, and underlying risk factors for instability.
Clinical Outcomes
Rate of dislocation and revision
According to a study using data from the Dutch Arthroplasty Register, 32-mm heads reduce
the risk of revision for dislocation compared with 22-mm and 28-mm heads for all surgical
approaches. In addition, 36-mm heads increasingly reduced the risk of revision for
dislocation but only for the posterolateral approach.35 Another study using data from the
Dutch Arthroplasty Registry study showed no difference in the overall rate of revision
between heads that were 32 mm or smaller, and heads that were 32 mm or larger.36
This finding may indicate that 32 mm is the ideal head size in patients with standard
dislocation risk profiles. Additional research is necessary.
Selection of femoral head size requires a balance between increased hip stability and wear.

Conclusions
Using a larger femoral head size is one of several strategies that can help reduce the risk of
THA instability by increasing the head-neck ratio to reduce impingement and increase the
jump distance; however, larger heads also are associated with volumetric wear, thinner
polyethylene liners, and taper corrosion (Figure 4). In contemporary THA, head sizes of 32 mm
and 36 mm appear to balance these issues appropriately. Selection between the two sizes
should be based on final acetabular component size, (which determines polyethylene
thickness), patient age, and patient risk factors for instability.
Elevated Rim, Face-Changing, and Lateralized Polyethylene
Liners
Background
Modularity in THA permits multiple polyethylene liner options to reduce THA instability
intraoperatively or to manage a patient with a dislocation who requires revision surgery
(Figure 5).
Elevated (lipped) liners
Face-changing (oblique) liners
Lateralized (offset) liners

permission from Sheth NP, Melnic CM, Paprosky WG: Evaluation and management of chronic
total hip instability. Bone Joint J 2016;98[1 suppl A]:44-49.)

Background
This type of liner is recognized by the stepped nature of the acetabular liner rim that
adds extra height to the shell in one location to improve jump distance. This extra height
most often is positioned in the posterosuperior quadrant of the acetabulum to increase
the jump distance at the position of greatest dislocation risk; however, a recent study
suggested that the posteroinferior quadrant may be more beneficial.37
Designed to have a smooth variation in liner height above the acetabular rim, often
designated as an angle (eg, 10°), this type of liner allows for alteration of the anteversion
of a well-fixed acetabular component to increase stability.
Characterized by polyethylene components that have extra material between the
acetabular component and the surface on which the femoral head articulates, this type
of liner often is designated as a plus-number (eg, + 4 mm). These liners primarily are

11/31

designed to increase offset to help with soft-tissue tensioning, but they also change the
center of rotation of the hip relative to the acetabular component. They also increase leg
length, whereas most high-offset femoral stems increase only offset. These liners
commonly are used to lateralize the hip joint center of rotation and restore offset if the
acetabular component position is medialized, as with protrusio defects.38
Indications
Elevated, face-changing, and lateralized liners are available for most modern implant systems
and may include a combination of features to achieve a desired result (eg, + 4, 10° tilted liner).
Elevated liners may increase the range of motion arc before component impingement;39,40
however, a contradictory study reported damage to the polyethylene over time because of
impingement.41
Isolated single component revision

Indications
In patients who undergo revision for instability with an ingrown acetabular component
within the acceptable range of component position, elevated and face-changing liners
can be used to make small corrections to component positioning to improve hip
stability42-44 without the morbidity and difficulty45 of explanting a well-fixed acetabular
component.46
Clinical Outcomes
Dislocation risk
Elevated and lateralized liners reduce the risk of dislocation in certain patient populations.47-
49 A recent study suggested that the use of elevated, oblique, or lateralized liners in patients
with recurrent instability increases the risk of re-dislocation.50
Wear rates

No increase in wear rates has been observed with elevated liners;51 however, increased
linear and volumetric wear has been observed with lateralized liners.49,52,53
Aseptic loosening
No increase in loosening rates has been observed with elevated liners.47
Lateralized liners may increase loosening rates in acetabular components that are not yet
ingrown in patient who underwent primary and revision THA;54 however, one study refuted
this finding.49 Archibeck et al54 found that lateralized liners increased the loosening rate
from 0.12% to 4.2% in patients who underwent primary THA and from 1.7% to 7% in patients
who underwent revision THA.
Face-changing liners
Currently, limited evidence is available in the literature about the efficacy or safety of face-
changing liners, which may be an area of future study.
Conclusions
Several polyethylene liner options are available to help reduce the risk of THA instability or to
treat a patient with recurrent instability via modular bearing exchange. In general, these liner
options should be considered only if small corrections are necessary to achieve hip joint
stability or restore anatomic reconstruction. For primary THA, optimal component positioning
and the placement of a neutral liner is preferred in most patients.
Dual-Mobility Constructs
Background
Dual mobility as a bearing choice
Dual mobility is relatively new to the US market and has been rapidly increasing in popularity
for primary and revision surgery.
Although dual mobility is new in the United States, it has been used successfully for many
years in Europe.
Boyer et al55 recently published a 22-year follow-up of 240 THA implants that received a
monoblock, dual mobility construct and found a dislocation rate of zero and implant
survival rate of 81.4%.
Dual mobility constructs
The acetabular shell of the dual mobility construct can be monoblock or modular.

How dual mobility works
Biomechanically, dual mobility works to increase hip stability via two main principles:
increased arc of motion before impingement and larger jump distance (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Drawings show total hip arthroplasty implant options. A, B, and C show a dual
mobility cup with a metal cup (black), a polyethylene liner (grey), and a head/neck (white). D
and E show a standard fixed-liner implant. During motion with a dual mobility cup, the neck
impinges with the liner, causing rotation in the unconstrained joint between the liner and the
metal cup (B). Subluxation occurs if the neck impinges with the metal cup or in cases of
extra-articular impingement (C). Because of a more favorable and effective head-neck ratio,
dual mobility cups (B) permit a larger range of motion compared with fixed-liner implants (D),
in which dislocation occurs earlier (E). (Reproduced with permission from Grazioli A, Ek ET,
Rüdiger HA: Biomechanical concept and clinical outcome of dual mobility cups. Int Orthop
2012;36[12]:2411-2418.)

Background
In monoblock constructs, the acetabular shell typically is made of highly polished cobalt-
chromium or stainless steel with an outer surface treatment to facilitate bony ongrowth
(Figure 7). A ceramic or cobalt-chromium femoral head is constrained within and
articulates with the polyethylene liner, which then articulates with the acetabular shell.
No acetabular screws can be used with a monoblock shell.
Figure 7 Photograph shows a monoblock, dual mobility total hip arthroplasty system. A,
Acetabular shell. B, Polyethylene insert. C, Femoral head. The solid acetabular shell
prevents the use of screws. (Adapted with permission from Dubin JA, Westrich GH:
Anatomic dual mobility compared to modular dual mobility in primary total hip
arthroplasty: A matched cohort study. Arthroplast Today 2019;5[4]:509-514.)
A modular, dual mobility system works in a similar manner, except that a highly polished
cobalt-chromium liner is impacted into a titanium acetabular shell (Figure 8). This
additional metal-on-metal articulation allows for the use of acetabular screws and is
associated with the advantage of modularity (ie, a dual mobility liner can be placed into a
compatible, well-fixed acetabular shell at the time of revision surgery). Some surgeons
have expressed theoretic concerns that modular, dual mobility systems may be

associated with mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC) from the cobalt-
chromium liner and the titanium acetabular shell interface.
Figure 8 Photograph shows a modular dual mobility total hip arthroplasty system. A,
Acetabular shell. B, Cobalt-chromium liner. C, Polyethylene insert. D, Femoral head. Note
the screw holes in the acetabular shell and the addition of the cobalt-chromium liner

(Reproduced with permission from Dubin JA, Westrich GH: Anatomic dual mobility

study. Arthroplast Today 2019;5[4]:509-514.)
The arc of motion before impingement is increased via its dual articulation and a larger
head-neck ratio. Most of the motion is theorized to occur at the interface of the inner
femoral head with the polyethylene liner. After this inner range of motion has been
maximized, the polyethylene liner will articulate with the acetabular shell to provide
additional arc of motion.56
Because the inner head is constrained within the polyethylene liner, the jump distance
becomes that of the polyethylene liner, which is much larger than that of femoral heads
used in typical hard-on-soft bearings. This increased jump distance and the increased arc
of motion before impingement provide more security against dislocation.57
Indications
Reduce the risk of instability after revision THA
Decrease dislocation rates for THA performed to manage femoral neck fractures

9/3/26, 7:26 AM

16/31

Reduce THA instability in patients with decreased spinopelvic motion

Indications
The incidence of revision THA continues to increase, and revision THA is associated with
dislocation rates ranging from 10% to 28%.58 A retrospective analysis of 315 patients
who underwent revision THA with the use of a modular, dual mobility construct for the
management of instability, aseptic loosening, or conversion THA noted a dislocation rate
of 3.8%. The authors concluded that dual mobility constructs may be a good option to
prevent instability after revision THA.59
Patients who undergo THA for the management of a femoral neck fracture have an
increased risk for dislocation compared with patients who undergo THA for the
management of osteoarthritis. Historic data show a dislocation risk as high as 10% if THA
is performed via a posterior approach to manage a displaced femoral neck fracture.60 A
prospective multicenter study from Europe showed a substantially lower dislocation rate
(1.4%) with the use of a dual mobility construct via the posterior approach in 214
patients with a displaced femoral neck fracture.61
The hip-spine relationship has become better understood in the past few years. A cohort
of patients with decreased spinopelvic mobility have an increased risk for dislocation. A
recent meta-analysis showed that patients with a history of spinal fusion who underwent
THA had a more than twofold increased risk of dislocation compared with a cohort of
patients without lumbar pathology.62 Currently, some surgeons recommend dual
mobility constructs for patients with a higher risk for dislocation. In a recent series of 86
patients with a history of lumbar fusion of two or more levels who underwent THA with
the use of a dual mobility construct, Chalmers et al63 reported a dislocation-free survival
rate of 100% at a follow-up of 2 years.
Clinical Outcomes
Dual mobility dislocation rates
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:26 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002061
17/31

Dual mobility constructs are associated with additional risks compared with standard bearings.
MACC
Increased osteolysis/polyethylene wear
Increased linear wear rates have been observed with dual mobility polyethylene liners.
Linear penetration of 1.59 mm per year and 1.07 mm per year have been reported at 1 year
and 2 years postoperatively, respectively.64 These rates are substantially higher than the
reported rates of 0.1 mm per year for traditional ceramic-on–highly cross-linked polyethylene
bearings.65
Osteolysis also is a concern after dual mobility THA. In a study of 2,480 monoblock, dual
mobility THA procedures performed between 1998 and 2003, Combes et al66 reported a low
dislocation rate (0.88%) but also noted a 6% rate of osteolysis. This rate of osteolysis
increased to 13% in patients younger than 50 years at the time of surgery.
Risk of intraprosthetic dislocation

Clinical Outcomes
A 2017 meta-analysis of a cohort of 17,908 THA implants demonstrated dislocation rates
of 0.9% and 3.0% if a dual mobility construct was used for primary and revision THA,
respectively. In addition, intraprosthetic dislocation rates of 0.7% and 1.3% were
reported for primary and revision THA, respectively.67 These rates fall below the
historical dislocation rates associated with more traditional bearing surfaces.
One of the primary concerns with modular, dual mobility constructs is that they may
involve the use of a cobalt-chromium-titanium taper junction, which may lead to MACC,
which is similar to the wear observed in patients with trunnionosis. Elevated serum
metal ion levels have been observed in as many as 25% of patients with modular, dual
mobility articulations, and pseudotumor has been observed in 50% of symptomatic
patients.68 A recent retrieval analysis performed at the Mayo Clinic demonstrated
backside burnishing and corrosive wear in 11 of 12 modular, dual mobility liners
removed at the time of revision surgery.69
Intraprosthetic dislocation occurs if the inner cobalt-chromium or ceramic head
dislodges from the outer polyethylene liner. Intraprosthetic dislocation has been
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:26 AM
AAOS | Bearing Surface Options: Wear, Stability, and Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002061
18/31

theorized to most often occur during the reduction of a dislocated dual mobility hip.
During reduction, the outer polyethylene liner catches the edge of the acetabular shell,
and the inner head levers out of the liner. Often, the inner head is then reduced within
the shell, but the outer polyethylene liner is left behind in the soft tissues. This process
may lead to catastrophic wear and/or failure from the cobalt-chromium or ceramic
femoral head articulating on the metal acetabular shell. In a recent study, seven
dislocations were observed in a cohort of 154 dual mobility constructs (mostly used in
patients with a high risk for dislocation). Of these seven dislocations, five included an
intraprosthetic dislocation on attempted bedside reduction in the emergency
department under propofol sedation. Based on these data, Addona et al70
recommended that the reduction of any dual mobility dislocation occur in the operating
room under general or spinal anesthesia, with fluoroscopy backup and a low threshold
for open reduction.
Conclusions
Dual mobility constructs have been proven to reduce dislocation rates, and their use has
drastically increased in the United States. However, they are associated with risks of
intraprosthetic dislocation, increased polyethylene wear rates, and MACC in modular designs.
Data on the long-term survival of dual mobility constructs, particularly modular designs, are
lacking; this topic is certain to be the subject of future study. A dual mobility construct is best
supported in revision THA and primary THA in patients with a high risk for instability. The more
general use of dual mobility constructs in primary THA remains a subject of active debate.
Constrained Liners
Background
Patients with recurrent instability, who have undergone multiple prior hip surgeries, or with
abductor deficiency present a substantial challenge, and their treatment frequently requires
salvage techniques.
Salvage options include constrained acetabular liners (CALs), dual mobility constructs,
trochanteric advancement, muscle transfers, Girdlestone resection arthroplasty, and
nonsurgical management.

In general, these problems are surgical, and nonsurgical treatment is reserved best for
patients who cannot undergo surgical treatment secondary to medical issues and patients
who do not have substantial pain or neurovascular compromise.
The abductor muscle complex (primarily the gluteus medius) is the most important dynamic
stabilizer of the hip joint and is critical for THA stability and function.
Patients with abductor deficiency have an increased risk for recurrent dislocations and may
require specialized techniques to achieve THA stability.
CALs were initially developed to address the challenge of recurrent THA instability and
abductor deficiency.
CALs function by capturing the femoral head.
Most contemporary constrained liners use a large polyethylene build-up that extends
beyond the equator of the femoral head and is protected by a locking ring (Figure 5).
In general, the liner can be placed directly into the acetabular component using the normal
locking mechanism of the acetabular shell. Alternatively, the polyethylene liner can be
cemented into the acetabular shell in patients with incompatible locking mechanisms or
malpositioned acetabular components that are not readily amenable to acetabular
component revision because of extensive bone loss or large, well-fixed revision
components already in place.
The femoral head must then snap into the polyethylene liner, and the locking ring around
the rim of the CAL must be secured (Figure 9).

At the point of impingement, greater force is required to lever out the femoral head,
reducing the risk of dislocation.
In patients with abductor deficiency, this capture mechanism protects against the loss of the
dynamic soft-tissue tensioning provided by the gluteus medius.
By design, the available arc of motion is decreased because the polyethylene extends beyond
the equator of the femoral head.
Therefore, the functional arc of motion is reduced, mandating appropriate component
positioning in placing CALs.
Increased impingement of the components results in greater forces distributed through the
locking mechanism and the bone-implant interface.
Larger femoral heads can improve the arc of motion before impingement.
Modifications to some specific component designs have been made to improve the
functional arc of motion.
Indications
CALs are a salvage option for revision THA in patients with recurrent instability, neuromuscular
disorders, cognitive impairment, or abductor deficiency with extensive soft-tissue compromise.
The most widely accepted use of CALs is in patient with disruption of the soft-tissue envelope
and abductor deficiency; however, the amount of soft-tissue compromise necessary to
warrant a CAL is poorly characterized.
In general, fully ingrown, and well-positioned components are necessary before the placement
of a CAL.
Given the reduced arc of motion observed with CALs, appropriate component positioning is
critical to preserve functional hip range of motion and minimize impingement, which may
lead to early catastrophic failure.
Placement of a CAL into a well-fixed acetabular component is preferred.
Implantation of a CAL into a newly inserted acetabular component may result in failure of
osteointegration and aseptic loosening from the increased strain at the component-bone

If the acetabular component must be revised and a CAL is necessary, two options are
available.
A staged approach, which involves the initial placement of the revised acetabular
component, followed by a second procedure to insert the CAL after the component has
fully ingrown. In general, this approach is preferred by most surgeons given the potential
reduction in loosening rates.
Placement of the CAL acutely at the time of acetabular component revision, which
requires multiple additional screws to secure the shell, followed by extended
postoperative restrictions to limit weight bearing, activities, and hip range of motion. This
option avoids a second procedure; however, it also may be associated with an increased
risk of aseptic loosening. If selecting this option, a porous metal shell with multiple screws
may enhance fixation.71
Clinical Outcomes
CALs are considered a salvage option to manage a complex clinical challenge in a very high-risk
patient population.
Therefore, reported clinical outcomes reflect the complexity of the situation and
demonstrate a high rate of long-term failure.
Early results have been more encouraging.
The primary mode of failure is impingement.72
The force at the point of impingement may overcome the containment force of the implant,
resulting in dislocation of the femoral head from the liner.
In addition, repetitive impingement events transfer shear forces to the other interfaces of
the construct, including the liner-cup or cup-bone interface, which may result in catastrophic
failure at any of these locations.
Short-term to midterm outcomes demonstrate a reasonable success rate; however, long-term
data confirm a high incidence of loosening and re-dislocation. These outcomes appears to
reflect the complex nature of CAL placement in this patient population.
In a systematic review that included 2,852 patients who received a CAL, the mean dislocation
and/or failure rate was 11.4% at a follow-up of 4.3 years.73
In a study of 58 hips that underwent implantation of a CAL, Chalmers et al74 observed a 19%
(11 hips) re-dislocation rate at a mean follow-up of 3.5 years, and revision for any reason was
required in 24% (14 hips) of the cohort. In patients who underwent modular exchange for the

A report of 55 patients treated with the use of a CAL during revision THA reported a re-

In a series of 755 consecutive CALs with a minimum follow-up of 10 years, survivorship for
the entire cohort was 68.5% (517 CALs) and 51.7% (390 CALs) at a follow-up of 5 years and 10

instability, of which 28.9% (37 hips) experienced failure with re-dislocation. The overall
survivorship for the latter group was 47.7% at final follow-up.76
Conclusions
CALs represent an important salvage option for revision THA to manage recurrent instability
and abductor deficiency. If constrained liners are implanted at the time of modular exchange,
the retained acetabular component must be fully ingrown and in an optimal position. The
primary mode of failure is impingement, resulting in excessive forces distributed to the
component interfaces. Early results are encouraging; however, long-term follow-up has
demonstrated a high rate of failure secondary to loosening and re-dislocation.
